did_you_know.text: Isaiah is commanded to proclaim the word of the Lord clearly and boldly: to declare the people’s transgressions and the sins of the house of Jacob.
The people are described as seeking the Lord every day and desiring to know His ways, but the rest of the chapter reveals a gap between their religious appearance and their moral conduct.
The people ask why their fasting and self-denial receive no answer, but the prophet replies that on their fast days they continue to pursue their own affairs and exploit their workers.
Isaiah emphasizes that fasting accompanied by quarrels, strife, and violence is not the kind of fasting that makes one’s voice heard on high.
Bowing the head, wearing sackcloth, and sitting in ashes do not by themselves make a day an acceptable fast before the Lord; moral conduct is also required.
The fast that the Lord chooses includes breaking the chains of wickedness, undoing the bonds of the yoke, setting the oppressed free, and breaking every yoke of oppression.
The acceptable fast is also expressed through practical acts of kindness: sharing bread with the hungry, bringing the poor into one’s home, covering the naked, and caring for needy relatives.
Isaiah describes the results of righteousness and kindness through images of the dawn’s light, healing, righteousness going before a person, and the glory of the Lord gathering them in.
God’s answer is connected with removing the yoke, stopping the pointing finger and accusations against others, and giving up malicious speech; then it says, “Here I am.”

At the end of the chapter, keeping the Sabbath is also emphasized as part of the restoration: one must refrain from pursuing personal interests and speaking ordinary words, and honor the Sabbath as a day of delight and holiness.
